concepts.label: Training data
concepts.summary: The examples a model learns from. Performance on this set tells you what the model memorised, not what it learned.

source_spans.quote: The training set is the portion of the data the model sees during fitting.

misconceptions.statement: If it does well on the training data, it is a good model.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Training accuracy is the first and often only number a beginner sees, and high numbers usually mean success everywhere else in life.
misconceptions.correction: Training accuracy measures recall of examples already seen. A model can score perfectly by memorising and still be useless on anything new.

concepts.label: Generalisation
concepts.summary: A model generalises when it performs well on data it has never seen. This, not training accuracy, is the goal.

source_spans.quote: Generalisation is the ability to perform well on previously unseen inputs.

misconceptions.statement: Any model will generalise if you give it enough data.
misconceptions.why_plausible: More data does help in many cases, so it reads as a universal fix rather than one factor among several.
misconceptions.correction: Data volume does not rescue a model whose capacity lets it memorise. Capacity and regularisation matter independently of size.

concepts.label: Overfitting
concepts.summary: A model overfits when it captures noise specific to the training set. Training error keeps falling while error on new data rises.

source_spans.quote: Overfitting occurs when a model fits noise in the training data rather than the underlying signal.
The characteristic signature is a widening gap between training and validation error.

misconceptions.statement: 99 percent on training means roughly 99 percent on new data.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Nothing in the training run signals a problem. The number goes up and up, which looks exactly like progress.
misconceptions.correction: The two scores decouple once the model starts fitting noise. A near-perfect training score with no validation check is the classic warning sign, not a result.

misconceptions.statement: Overfitting means the data was dirty.
misconceptions.why_plausible: The word noise sounds like a data quality problem rather than a model capacity problem.
misconceptions.correction: Overfitting is about the model having enough capacity to memorise whatever it is given. Clean data can be overfit just as easily.

concepts.label: Validation split
concepts.summary: Holding out data the model never trains on, so you can measure generalisation instead of guessing at it.

source_spans.quote: A held-out validation set provides an unbiased estimate of performance on unseen data.

misconceptions.statement: You can tune your model against the test set as long as you do not train on it.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Tuning does not feel like training, so the test set still seems untouched.
misconceptions.correction: Repeated tuning against a set leaks information into your choices. The score stops being an honest estimate even though no gradient touched it.

concepts.label: Regularisation
concepts.summary: Constraining a model so it prefers simpler explanations, trading a little training accuracy for better performance on new data.

source_spans.quote: Regularisation penalises model complexity, biasing the fit toward simpler hypotheses.

misconceptions.statement: Regularisation improves the model with no downside.
misconceptions.why_plausible: It is presented as the fix for overfitting, so it reads as strictly good.
misconceptions.correction: Regularisation deliberately raises training error. Too much of it underfits. The trade is the whole point.
